Insufficient cooling may be causing performance throttling in i9-powered MacBooks. Form over function wins again.

Apple was kind of forced into an inconvenient position by Intel. People all want the new and shiny processors, but the core count increase as well as the frequency increases across the board have made the new processors run hotter and require more power than had previously been the case. Apple having just slimmed down their notebooks, expecting efficiency improvements, not regression, got kind of fucked when the new generation came out.

Many of the other manufacturers on the Windows side of the spectrum have had to redesign their cooling solutions, and Dell's XPS for example still can not deal with the i9, which is enormously power-hungry and very hot-headed. Very few of the thing & light notebooks are actually capable of dealing with it, so it comes as no surprise that the MacBook Pro's can't do it either, though the performance gain overall is disappointing to say the least.

Of course the blow could have been weakened by improving the cooling solution. However this would have required a complete redesign of the Macbook chassis, and Apple is currently mid-cycle, with a redesign expected for 2020 at the earliest. With WWDC having passed and People anxiously (and angrily) waiting for a MacBook Pro refresh, a redesign was out of the question because they were already behind and the time for large announcements had already passed with WWDC. However they had to release something at this point in time.

As such it is at least somewhat understandable to me that Apple decided to appease the people waiting for a new machine right now by releasing a silent update with the new processor generation. They even threw in DDR4 RAM, even though they previously were rigorously against it, probably to appease people for the time being, giving them a slightly bigger timeframe to figure out the next big redesign.

It is highly likely that Apple will bring out a redesigned chassis with an adapted cooling solution once the new 10nm processor hit. However Intel has been having massive problems regarding the node shrink, and so it is probably the best move strategically from Apple to wait until a fitting 10nm part hits the market and release a major redesign and update at that point, which right now is very much looking like 2020. Unless AMD somehow manages to release a 10nm competitor to the current Intel mobile processors in the 45 and 28 Watt brackets, I reckon we'll be stuck with this latest update for quite a while, unsatisfactory as it may be.

In most cases, this is correct. When you need more power, you will need a more capable thermal solution and thus more space. I can not speak for the aesthetics of a device with a larger volume as that is quite subjective, but generally if you want more performance, you will have to make some tradeoffs. Weight is one of them, as is Volume. It is simply more challenging to fit an i9 into a Macbook than it is fitting it into a 8lbs plastic bomber (at acceptable temperatures). Apple is striving towards fitting the same performance into a smaller chassis, but is not easy and they are hitting some bumps in their journey.

If this was once case of their laptops having issues, I'd let it slide. But this is the second major recent issue that's come from them poorly engineering their laptops.

Most generations of the Macbook lineup had one or another flaw, some more serious than others, e.g. the GPU's dying in the 2011's or the screen peeling off in 2013/2014 lineup. But every other manufacturer also has problems like this. Dell's issue is (rather consistently) thermal management, Razer has Q/A issues, the list goes on. Nobody ever produces anything that is perfect, and everytime you roll out something new, there is a chance that it breaks. In most cases, manufacturers listen and they improve in the next generation, as Apple has done here. They have also created new problems, and they will likely address them in the next generation. But for that to happen there has to be some loud, clear and reasonable feedback. In this case the main point is "fix your damn thermal solution".

I am not defending Apple here, I am trying to shed some light on how they (presumably) made their decisions. Objectively, the i9 was a bad idea in the current form factor. The pricing is also quite hefty. These are things to be criticised and they should be fixed. Apple was not in a position to fix them right now, so they did the best they could within their capabilities without breaking everything apart. Let's hope that some loud criticism will make them hit us with a sane redesign earlier than speculated.
